intro: How the yearly ISA allowance applies to Cash ISAs, the lower cash limit planned for under-65s from 6 April 2027, and the rules meant to stop it being avoided.
explanation:
## One allowance covers all your adult ISAs

The {fact:isa_allowance} annual limit is not a separate allowance for each type of adult ISA. It is the total you can pay into your Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs) in a tax year, and money paid into a Cash ISA uses up part of the same allowance that a stocks and shares ISA draws on. A Lifetime ISA has a lower yearly limit of its own, but what you pay into it still counts towards the total. Junior ISAs have a separate allowance.

This limit is set to stay at {fact:isa_allowance} until April 2031.

## From 6 April 2027, under-65s face a lower cash limit

From 6 April 2027, anyone under 65 will be able to put no more than {fact:cash_isa_limit_under_65_2027} a year into cash ISAs, under ISA regulations due to come into force that day. People aged 65 or over can still use the whole {fact:isa_allowance} for cash ISAs.

The lower figure sits inside the overall allowance. An under-65 could therefore still use the rest of the allowance on a stocks and shares ISA.

## Extra rules aim to stop the cash limit being sidestepped

Three safeguards are due from 6 April 2027. First, cash held inside a stocks and shares ISA or an Innovative Finance ISA will have a flat-rate charge taken from the interest it earns. Second, investors under 65 cannot move money from those ISAs into a cash ISA. Third, a stocks and shares ISA cannot be invested entirely in money market funds.
